zone: North-side peaks of the Mountain Loop and the Stillaguamish
_areas_note: FIVE SEPARATE ROADS, not one zone road: Whitehorse from the Mine Road south off SR 530 west of Darrington (Niederprum trail); Three Fingers from Tupso Pass at the end of Road 41, which leaves the Mountain Loop near Verlot and runs north for roughly 18 miles; Big Four from the Big Four Picnic Area on the paved loop; Pilchuck from the Mount Pilchuck road above Verlot. A party cannot combine two of these in a weekend without a long drive back down to the valley. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE GROUPING. (1) BEDAL PEAK IS REMOVED. Its trailhead is Bedal Creek off the UNPAVED upper Mountain Loop on the Sauk River side, beyond Barlow Pass and closer to Sloan Peak and Monte Cristo than to anything on the Stillaguamish; it is already served by the Bedal Campground entry in the earlier upper-loop file and belongs with that group. (2) PILCHUCK IS KEPT BUT HAS TWO TRAILHEADS, NOT ONE. The standard route leaves the end of the Mount Pilchuck road as stated, but the East Ridge / Iodine Gulch line starts from the Bear Lake and Pinnacle Lake trailhead on a different spur road off the loop east of Verlot, and reaches the Bathtub Lakes basin from below. Pilchuck is also a STATE CONSERVATION AREA rather than national forest, though its trailhead sits on forest land and takes the federal pass. LAND STATUS SPLITS THE ZONE: Whitehorse and Three Fingers are inside the Boulder River Wilderness, which requires NO permit of any kind to camp; Big Four and Pilchuck are south of the highway and in no wilderness at all. NOT DUPLICATED from the earlier files: the Verlot corridor campgrounds, Bedal Campground, Barlow Pass, Monte Cristo, Gothic Basin, Clear Creek, Squire Creek. Also noted for the route data rather than for camping — the lookout stands on the SOUTHERNMOST of the three summits, so a route filed as the North Peak lookout route is describing the south peak.

sites.name: Three Fingers Lookout, south summit
sites.capacity: First come, first served, and small. A single sleeping platform takes two comfortably; the floor absorbs another two or three on pads, and parties have squeezed six to eight in at the cost of everyone's night. Treat four as the realistic number and anything above six as an emergency. THERE IS NOWHERE TO PITCH A TENT OUTSIDE — the cabin occupies the whole blasted summit block, so a full lookout means descending.
sites.water: None at the lookout. The last dependable water is the tarns and runnels around Goat Flats and the snowmelt near the gap below; above that you are melting snow off the glacier or carrying it. Plan on hauling several litres per person up the final stretch and expect to melt if you arrive late in a dry summer.
sites.permit: No permit and no reservation, and none is available — it cannot be booked. Inside the Boulder River Wilderness, which requires no self-issue permit to camp. A federal recreation pass is the parking requirement at forest trailheads on this side. Campfires are prohibited the whole way from the lake below up to the peak, and there is nothing to burn at the top anyway. The cabin is volunteer-maintained: leave it swept, close the shutters and the door properly against weather and rodents, pack out every scrap including food waste, and do not take or move anything belonging to it. If it has been closed for repair, stay out.
sites.notes: This is the reason to come here overnight and it is genuinely one of the few summit cabins in the state a climbing party can sleep in. It sits on the southernmost of the three summits, on ground that was blasted flat to seat it, and the final approach to the door is a set of steep wooden ladders bolted against the cliff — vertical, exposed, and not somewhere to be carrying a loose pack or moving in the dark. Getting to them means crossing the glacier on the peak's north side above the gap, which is a real crossing rather than a snowfield walk: axe and crampons all year, a rope and the ability to use it, and late in the season a moat between ice and rock that some parties follow instead, when they can find its entrance. It has been rebuilt and repaired repeatedly by volunteers over the decades, most recently in the structure itself, so it is sound but spartan — bare boards, shutters, no stove worth relying on, no facilities. Coming as a climbing party rather than a hiking one, the sensible plan is to camp lower and go up light, because a full lookout at nine at night with the ladders behind you is a bad position.

sites.name: Tin Can Gap high camp
sites.capacity: A few small pitches on rock and snow at and just below the gap; one or two parties, not a group site
sites.water: Snowmelt only for most of the season, and nothing at all once the snow around the gap has gone. Assume you are melting or carrying from Goat Flats.
sites.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit required. Federal recreation pass to park. Campfires prohibited on this whole stretch of trail; there is no fuel here regardless.
sites.notes: The last flat ground before the glacier, roughly a mile short of the lookout, and the correct camp for a party that wants the summit block early and cold rather than soft. The maintained trail effectively ends here, so everything above is a bootpath, snow and the ladders. Its value is that it puts the glacier crossing and the ladders in the first hour of the day, when the snow is still firm — a real advantage over starting from the meadows two miles back. The cost is exposure: it is a gap, it catches weather, and there is nothing sheltering about it. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin vegetation, and take a hard look at whether the crossing above is in condition before committing to a camp that only makes sense if you go up.

sites.name: Goat Flats
sites.capacity: The main camping area on this approach — several established pockets spread through the meadows and around the tarns. It absorbs a fair number of parties but is genuinely crowded on summer and autumn weekends, and it is the overflow when the lookout is full.
sites.water: Reliable through most of the season from the tarns and small streams in the meadows, though the standing water is shallow and warms up late in summer. Treat everything. Later in a dry year the tarns shrink and the better water is the running melt above the flats.
sites.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. Federal recreation pass at the trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in the Goat Flats area and along this trail generally. Bears work this basin, so hard-sided or hung food storage is expected rather than optional.
sites.notes: Open subalpine meadow about two miles beyond the lake, and the default base for anything on Three Fingers — the lookout, the middle summit, or a look at the south face. From here the gap and the glacier are within a straightforward morning. It is also the honest fallback for a party that walked up hoping for a bunk in the lookout and found it occupied: about two miles back down from the ladders, which is a long but manageable retreat with headlamps. The meadow soil is thin and heavily used, so pitch on the bare established spots and not on fresh turf. Snow lies here well into summer and the meadows are boggy for weeks after it goes.

sites.name: Saddle Lake
sites.capacity: Small — a handful of spots in the timber and meadow near the lake, plus an old volunteer-built shelter at the meadow edge that should be treated as rough emergency cover rather than accommodation
sites.water: The lake, which is dependable all season and needs treating. This is the last easy water before the meadows above.
sites.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED within 200 feet of the shoreline, so the lakeside spots that look obvious are not all legal. Campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of the lake and along the trail above it.
sites.notes: About two and a half miles in from the road end, in dense timber, and low enough that it is a contingency rather than a plan for anyone climbing. It matters for two reasons. First, the road: the Tupso Pass road has a long washout history and has at times been cut miles short of the trailhead, leaving parties to walk or bike the road grade — when that is the situation the lake is as far as many get on day one. Second, it is where a party that started late, or turned around at the gap in bad conditions, can stop without pushing all the way out. Do not plan a Three Fingers climb from here; it is too low and too far. Bugs are heavy in early summer.

sites.name: Whitehorse high camp, benches near Lone Tree Pass
sites.capacity: Informal — a flat sheltered meadow just past the pass takes a couple of tents, with smaller pockets on benches nearby and more ground on the traverse east toward the small lake below the pass. One or two parties.
sites.water: Snowmelt in season and the small tarn below the pass on the traverse east; both are seasonal. By late summer this side dries out and there may be nothing, so carry up or plan to melt. There is no water on the trail below.
sites.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no permit to camp, no quota, no self-issue box. No fee at the trailhead, which is unusual for this area and reflects how minimal the parking is. Fires are a bad idea on this ground and are commonly banned outright in late summer.
sites.notes: This is the high camp for the Northwest Shoulder, and most parties who do not intend a twelve-to-sixteen hour car-to-car day use it. The route is around 6,000 to 7,000 feet of gain from a low trailhead and the lower trail is notoriously steep and brushy, so splitting it at the pass converts a punishing single day into two reasonable ones and puts the glacier and the exposed summit scrambling in the morning. The sheltered meadow just beyond the pass is the pick — trees break the wind and it looks straight at the summit. Everything about this approach depends on the Mine Road out of the highway west of Darrington: it is rough, narrow, overgrown enough to scratch a vehicle, and has had bridge and washout closures that push the start well down the hill and add road walking. Confirm how far you can drive before you plan the day. Early season with snow cover over the brush is much the better time; by late summer the glacier above develops crevasses and a large bergschrund and the brush below is at its worst.

sites.name: Whitehorse Community Park campground, Darrington
sites.capacity: A developed county campground with tent and equestrian sites on a large park property; nightly fee
sites.water: Developed park water in season; confirm before relying on it outside summer
sites.permit: COUNTY park, not national forest — a nightly fee applies and no federal or state pass does anything here. Seasonal: closed and winterized through the winter months, roughly mid-autumn to mid-spring, which rules it out for the spring snow season when Whitehorse is actually in condition.
sites.notes: The nearest developed drive-in base to the Mine Road, sitting just outside Darrington with the mountain itself directly in view, which makes it a useful place to look at conditions on the northwest side the evening before. Its real role is staging: the Niederprum trailhead has room for only a handful of vehicles and nothing else, so sleeping in town and driving up in the small hours is the usual pattern rather than camping at the road end. Because it is county-run its season and fees are set separately from the forest campgrounds and change independently of them. The winter closure is the catch — the best window for the Northwest Shoulder is spring, and the campground may not be open yet.

sites.name: Big Four north-side staging and base bivouac
sites.capacity: No established camp of any kind. The picnic area at the trailhead is DAY USE ONLY and camping there is not permitted; parties climbing the north side bivouac informally at the base of the face on the avalanche debris and boulder ground beyond the maintained path.
sites.water: Creeks draining the face run all season near the base, and the debris field itself is meltwater. Treat everything. There is no developed water at the picnic area.
sites.permit: Not inside any wilderness — this side of the highway is ordinary national forest with no camping permit requirement. A federal recreation pass is required to park at the picnic area. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer and are frequently forest-wide.
sites.notes: Big Four is a car-to-car objective by design: the trailhead sits at low elevation barely a mile from the base of a face that rises about 4,000 feet, so the climbing starts almost immediately and there is no approach worth camping to shorten. Parties on the north-side lines, including the long winter couloir routes, typically leave overnight gear at the base and go up and down in a push rather than carrying a bivouac onto the face, which is a considered choice on a wall this active — rockfall and avalanche off it are constant and audible through the night. That same activity is why this entry is a contingency and not a recommendation: sleeping under this face means sleeping under a debris cone that is there because things fall on it. Position any bivouac well out of the runout, not at the toe of the snow. THE ICE CAVES AT THE BASE ARE LETHAL and collapse every year — do not camp near them, on them, or in them, and stay off them entirely. The nearest legal drive-in beds are the developed campgrounds down the paved loop toward Verlot.

sites.name: Bathtub Lakes basin, east of Mount Pilchuck
sites.capacity: Informal sites among the small lakes and benches of the basin; a few parties, nothing developed
sites.water: The lakes and their outlets, dependable through the season and needing treatment. This is a wet basin, which is the whole reason it works as a camp.
sites.permit: The summit and upper mountain are a STATE CONSERVATION AREA rather than national forest, but this basin and the approach to it are forest land and no camping permit applies. The parking requirement at the trailheads on this mountain is the FEDERAL pass — a state Discover Pass is not valid at them, which catches people out because of the state park name. No fires on the state land above, and fire bans are routine below in late summer.
sites.notes: This is the only real camp on Pilchuck and it serves the east side rather than the standard route. It is reached from below, from the Bear Lake and Pinnacle Lake trailhead on a spur road off the loop east of Verlot, then up past the lower lake and into the gulch above — a loose, brushy, steep piece of ground with vegetation-pulling and poor rock that is the genuine difficulty of the East Ridge, not the ridge itself. Camping in the basin splits that so the gulch is climbed fresh. It has no bearing on the standard summit trail, which leaves the end of the Mount Pilchuck road on the other side of the mountain and is a straightforward day hike to the restored summit lookout with no camping along it and none needed. Treat this as a plan for the east side and as a contingency for anyone who commits to the gulch late and would rather not descend it in the dark.
